items.title: Years after they got married in-game to save money, these two Final Fantasy XIV players are getting married IRL
items.summary: Love always finds a way. The post Years after they got married in-game to save money, these two Final Fantasy XIV players are getting married IRL appeared first on Destructoid.
items.content:
A very awkward but equally wise soldier once said, "I think at any time, any place, people can fall in love with each other." Two Final Fantasy XIV players proved this little nugget of wisdom true this week, when their in-game union blossomed into real-life nuptials.

The happy couple, known on X as 404Eules and Koyuka28 , started as best friends who shared a passion for Final Fantasy XIV . As they explored Eorzea together, they eventually decided to get married. They didn't do it to roleplay as a married couple; they did it for in-game perks.

Marrying another player in Final Fantasy XIV (in-game, "entering an eternal bond") can be complicated, but it comes with plenty of perks. Chief among them are the Eternity Rings, a pair of in-game wedding rings that let one player teleport to the other's location whenever they like. FFXIV players often marry purely to get an Eternity Ring, and Eules and Koyuka28 were no exception. At first.

Once Eules and Koyuka28 had their Eternity Rings, I can only assume they went back to being friends who played Final Fantasy XIV for a while, using their in-game marriage magic to cut down on travel time. But eventually, their friendship grew into something deeper, and they decided the two wanted to spend the rest of their lives together.

By all accounts, the ceremony that followed was a love letter to the game that brought them together. To symbolize their in-game union crossing over into the real world, Eules and Koyuka28 commissioned, or were given, a pair of Soul Crystals (unique trinkets that let players upgrade their character class abilities) representing their in-game classes, Paladin and Dragoon. To no one's surprise, the final products are beautiful.

Since word of Eules and Koyuka28's union hit social media, the happy couple seem to have become minor celebrities within the Final Fantasy XIV community. Fellow FFXIV fans are coming together to wish the newlyweds well. Perhaps the greatest show of support came from none other than Jason Carles Miller, the singer/songwriter who lent his voice to several of FFXIV's most popular songs, including "Close in the Distance, which just happened to play at Eules and Koyuka28's wedding.

If Eules and/or Koyuka28 are reading this article, here's a big old congratulations from the rest of the Destructoid crew and me! May your lives, real and virtual, be filled with love, laughter, and sick loot.

items.title: Final Fantasy XIV shares the times for its Japan Fan Festival livestreams
Review: Final Fantasy XIV Online (Switch 2) - An Expansive Port That Demands Your Commitment
items.content:
Final Fantasy XIV Online has been through quite a rollercoaster journey over the years on its way to becoming one of the most respected MMOs in the industry. Its 2010 launch was a disaster, plagued with performance issues and shoddy design that torpedoed its reputation.

Rather than pulling the plug early, Square decided to swap in a new director to salvage it, leading to a reboot in 2013 called A Realm Reborn. Since then, the game has mostly gone from strength to strength across over a decade of expansions and is now in the process of building up its second major arc.

Though this isn’t the first time Square Enix has brought Final Fantasy XIV to console, it is the first time it’s come to a Nintendo platform, and I’m happy to report that it stuck the landing. The full fat experience is here in all its glory, giving you access to a high quality and addictive RPG experience that’s sure to be in the running for one of the most content-rich games ever produced for a handheld.

The narrative places you in the role of a self-insert character in the land of Eorzea who comes into the picture just as geopolitical tensions are on the rise. After a catastrophic war five years earlier, the expansionist Garlean Empire was repelled by the city-states comprising the Eorzean Alliance, but its leaders desire revenge and are winding up for another grab at ultimate control.

Amid this, you’re also told through a vision by a mysterious goddess of light named Hydaelyn that you’re her chosen champion, and she tasks you with finding six magical crystals to ward off the servants of an approaching darkness.

Thus, we set off on the early steps of what came to be called the Hydaelyn-Zodiark Saga, a four-part fantasy epic that should take you no less than two-hundred hours to complete, and that’s assuming that you beeline for the finale and engage in almost no side content. After all that, there’s then a whole other expansion that’s in the early stages of setting up the next ten-year arc.

Suffice to say, Final Fantasy XIV features one of the richest storylines available in a modern RPG, weaving together the subplots of various nations, factions, and supporting characters to make for an impressively complex and deep narrative.

The downside to this, however, is that the pacing can be all over the place. The 60-hour story of the base game alone is basically an extended exposition dump detailing all the major players in the world and setting the stage for the building conflict to come, meaning you spend a lot of time scrolling through line after line of unvoiced text from NPCs telling you about very interesting story beats that happened some other time offscreen.

This leads to a narrative experience with some incredible highs and disappointing lows. Once the plot picks up steam and starts focusing more on current events, there are lots of awesome character moments and payoffs that make all the time investment up to that point feel worth it. Yet between those moments, it can sometimes feel like the plot really takes its time focusing on largely irrelevant or uninteresting subjects that you simply have to endure to reach the good stuff.

Gameplay design follows the expected structure of an MMO, giving you an enormous living world to explore packed with jobs and levels to grind, side quests to fulfill, minigames to fool around with, dungeons to raid, and a massive story to gradually uncover.

As long as you stick to the Main Story Quest chain, you'll be toured around all the main points of interest in an area and progressively introduced to core mechanics and objectives at a measured pace. Side quest content then fills out the world with more detail and texture, though tons of the quest objectives admittedly boil down to 'bring me three boar skins' fetch quests.

A big part of what makes the gameplay loop so addicting is the versatility of your character, who can independently level dozens of jobs that fill out various combat and non-combat roles. In a combat role, your job is built around a growing variety of cooldown-based actions, echoing the classic Final Fantasy ATB system that blends turn-based and action gameplay.

Every combat job has its own distinct gimmicks and features, such as how the Thaumaturge operates by repeatedly shifting between two passive states that bolster either damage output or MP regeneration. Mechanics like this keep fights from feeling too much like you’re just watching cooldown icons on a hotbar, and there are enough distinguishing traits to make the various classes all feel like they’re worth experimenting with.

Non-combat roles are just as dynamic, even without the pressure of attacking foes. If you're working as a Goldsmith, you can create various bits of armour and jewellery, and it's much more involved than merely clicking the 'Craft' button on a menu after you have the materials.

items.title: FFXIV Same-Region Player Matching Starts on Japanese Data Centers
items.summary: The 7.57 FFXIV patch adds same-region player matching oh Japanese physical data centers and Beastmaster fixes.
items.content:
The 7.57 patch is now live in Final Fantasy XIV worldwide and makes a major change to the Japanese version of the MMORPG by allowing same-region player matching for that physical data center following the feature being promised at FFXIV Fan Fest Berlin 2026 . This only applies to Japan for now. It also means people playing in that region now can test out the new Visit Another World Server and see the new cross-world linkshells databases. There’s no word yet on when players in other regions might also get that feature.

This FFXIV same-region player matching change applies to all four logical data centers in the Japanese physical data center. This means people in the following worlds can now match in the Cross-world Linkshells, Crystalline Conflict Ranked Matches, Duty Finder, Fellowships, Party Finder, and PvP Teams. Their Friend List will now show Party Invites and Tells from folks in the physical data center, and the Free Companies will feature Chat functions.

The other adjustments in FFXIV patch 7.57 tend to be fixes or tied to the new Crucible Rankings Season 1 that starts on October 25, 2026. Beastmaster’s beasts will now change to face targets after being told to stay to ensure they’ll carry out subsequent orders. Capturing will also work as intended in Amdapor Keep, North Shroud, and The Tam-Tara Deepcroft (Hard).

Final Fantasy XIV is available for the Switch 2 , PS4, PS5, Xbox Series X, and PC, the FFXIV Evercold expansion will launch in January 2027, and the Japanese version now offers same-region player matching.

Everything We Know About Final Fantasy 14 Evercold So Far
items.summary: 8.0 is shaping up to be the biggest revamp of the MMORPG since A Realm Reborn
items.content:
We’re a little less than a month away from Final Fantasy XIV Fan Fest Tokyo which will likely contain some of the final major bits of info we’ll get on Evercold ahead of its January 2027 release. But even now, there’s still a lot we know about the expansion which is looking like the most significant update to the game and its systems since Creative Studio III literally blew up the world with A Realm Reborn 13 years ago. Here’s what we know.

Evercold will come with two new job classes and we’ve already seen the first—bastion. The bastion is a tank class wielding its signature weapon, the skyltborg. What’s that you ask? Imagine a gunblade, now make it a gunshield…that also has a blade. In the class’s brief overview trailer, you can see the skyltborg defend with giant shields, attack at range with bursts of aether fire, while also getting into melee range to dice shit up. It’s an unholy amalgamation of three different disciplines—melee dps, ranged dps, and tanking—that somehow manages to work. We haven’t had official confirmation of the second class, but we know it will feature ranged physical damage. Fan theories suggest the class involves a crossbow and PC Gamer has a neat breakdown that makes a strong case in support of that.

Perhaps the biggest draw to Final Fantasy XIV , beyond the at times legendary storytelling, is the incredible detail with which players can customize their avatar. With Evercold , the game is getting a wealth of new customization options including changing Au Ra horns, nose shadings, face paint, and custom color picking for eyes, hair, and skin tones. Additionally, customization options are also coming to animations giving players the ability to have unique looks for their teleport spell and other class-specific actions.

Evercold is really taking the theme of customization to heart because for the first time, players will be able to choose how they progress in the main story quest. Where in previous expansions unfolded linearly, Evercold will allow players to choose where they take the story next, and conversations with NPCs will reflect the choices they’ve made. In the example shared by Square Enix, a player finishes area A and has the choice of visit areas B, C, or D in any order. To make sure everything progresses smoothly no matter which choice players make, each area will automatically balance its content commensurate with player levels.

One of the biggest complaints about FFXIV of late his how samey all the classes feel. All tank, melee DPS, ranged DPS, and healer abilities feel like palette / flavor text swaps of the same four-five basic actions. It seems Square Enix have heard these gripes, revealing the new “evolved” combat system for Evercold which seeks to return a sense of individuality to the job classes by streamlining their abilities (which, in turn, helps out newer players by cutting down all the buttons and ability rotations they have to learn.) Square Enix hasn’t shared the “evolved” forms of every class yet, but there are a few out there with breakdowns of how the new abilities and combos will work. But if you’ve grown too used to the way things have always been done, FFXIV will keep the old ways in place with “reborn” mode.

Evercold will also rearrange how players spend their time to cut down on the massive grind as players level multiple job classes at the level cap. Currently, to keep up with the choco-bonses you have to complete daily quests to amass the currency you use to buy higher level gear. That system will go away in favor of a weekly system in which you choose quests you can complete on your own time that’ll award you activity points…used to buy higher level gear.

Another time sink is acquiring high level gear across multiple classes. It is tough when you play more than one job class, as each one requires a different set of gear and you gotta work for all that shit. Evercold attempts to cut through that never-ending hamster wheel by allowing players to “reflect” their gear with the highest item level (essentially the highest tier of gear you own) to their other max-level job classes. It won’t work for further gear enhancements like materia, so you still gotta work for your best-in-slot stuff, but it should still make it easier to bring your second and third job classes up to speed.

Your chocobo companion is your trusty steed. You do everything together with one big caveat, you can’t take them into dungeons with you. Evercold will change that, updating the companion system to allow chocobos as combat party members. This means, if you really hate waiting in the duty finder queue, you can run a dungeon with just one other person, your two chocobos taking up the final two slots.

items.title: New FFXIV Mouse and Mouse Pads Reference Regulators and The Arcadion Bosses
items.summary: The new Taito and Square Enix FFXIV Dawntrail mouse and mouse pads reference Solution Nine Regulators and The Arcadion Bosses.
items.content:
Square Enix and Taito announced a new collection of Final Fantasy XIV light up mouse and mouse pad pairs based on the FFXIV Dawntrail Solution Nine area Regulators and Arcadion Raid bosses . There are three mouse pad options available, with two heading to arcades as prizes in Japan everywhere and a Hot and Deep Blue variant only showing up as a Taito-exclusive. All of the options will show up in Japan at the end of October 2026. It’s unknown if we’ll see Square Enix sell them worldwide like other FFXIV mouse pads. Stores like Aitai Kuji are already taking pre-orders and will ship the items worldwide.

In the case of the FFXIV mouse, it features the Solution Nine Regulator design on the top. It is a wired mouse. When in use, the color will shift from red to blue to show if it is inactive or active. This is the same sort of color connotation used in-game. There is only one variant of that.

It’s the FFXIV Dawntrail Arcadion Raid boss mouse pads that look different. The standard options are one design that pairs up AAC Light-heavyweight M1 boss Black Cat with AAC Light-heavyweight M4 boss Wicked Thunder, while the other features the AAC Cruiserweight M1 boss Dancing Green. Meanwhile, the other Taito-exclusive design features the AAC Heavyweight M2 boss pair Red Hot and Deep Blue.

Here are the official images showing all of the designs ahead of their debut.

The Final Fantasy XIV light up Regulator mouse and Arcadion Raid boss mouse pads will show up in Japanese arcades as prizes at the end of October 2026, and FFXIV and the Dawntrail expansion are on the Switch 2, PS4, PS5, Xbox Series X, and PC.

items.title: Final Fantasy XIV’s latest patch basically starts Evercold, but only gives you a short taste
items.content:
I know I said last time we’ve officially entered Evercold, but you can take that statement even more literally with patch 7.56. The MSQ for this patch is short but sweet, taking the Warrior of Light, Alphinaud, and Estinien to the fourth. There, we’re trapped on a deserted island, attacked by some strange machines, and saved by what is no doubt a teaser for the new ranged job to be revealed at the Tokyo Fan Fest. I won’t spoil it here, but it looks cool even if it isn’t exactly what I wanted. (I wanted something using Vanille’s whip staff thing from FFXIII, but maybe next time.) There’s unfortunately no dungeon or trial this time around, just two instanced battles, but both are a good time and interesting enough to engage you. The outfit you get at the end of the MSQ this time is also fantastic, and I’ve been using it as my Beastmaster outfit.

The focus of my time with this patch instead has been squarely on Beastmaster, the new Limited Job. As one of the few who love playing Blue Mage, I was stoked to have something similar again, and it seems a lot more people are enjoying this new job than did Blue Mage. That’s for good reason, as Beastmaster seems to focus way more on solo, open-world content instead of needing to go through party finder to get a group together for a dungeon. There is still some of that here, but most of the monsters you can tame are out in Eorzea.

More than anything, it’s nice to have something to do in these old zones again. I’ve been hunting down monsters to add to my besti-beastiery, fighting random mobs for experience, and running FATEs with other random players. That part alone is a lot of fun, but Beastmaster has its own unique gameplay style unlike any other job, even back when Summoner was actually a pet class. The basic loop for Beastmaster has you summon one of your three chosen monsters, then you and your companion attack an enemy to build up your respective TP bars. Once one of you reaches 100 TP, you can use a special color-coded attack, which will then reset your TP back to 0. Every monster only has one color attack, while you have all four at your disposal. To do some real damage, you need to follow up the first attack with the next in the sequence, shown going clockwise on your job gauge. So if you do a green move, your monster needs to use red, for example. Either one of you can start or end the combo too, but you still need to go in clockwise order to gain any bonus effects.

You’re not just waiting around to build up these combos, as there’s still a lot to consider in the moment-to-moment combat, even if it is overall slower-paced than the typical jobs in the game. When summoning a monster to the field, you gain the One with Nature buff, which allows you to use either Borrow or Tempered Release. Borrow lets you gain a special action based on the monster’s species for the duration they are on the field, while Tempered Release has your monster perform their unique skill. You can only use one per summon, so you need to choose wisely. You might want to borrow a cool dodge move that also grants you evasion up for a bit to dodge some incoming AoEs, or you might want your monster’s special healing skill for some more survivability overall. It’s a cool system even if it’s difficult to keep track of all the moving parts.

That difficult to keep track of theme continues in Beastmaster’s special solo content, the Crucible of the Unbroken. This is something of a rogue-like mode, where you move between spaces on a board game, with each space representing an encounter. You can pick a number of Beasties to join you on a board, but again, only three per battle, and all HP persists between encounters. You need to consider what monsters in your party will do the most damage or be the most survivable, when to use special items that grant healing, revives, or special buffs, and what temporary equipment you want to equip. It’s kind of a lot, but having only gone through the first board so far, it's a lot of fun too.

Overall, I’ve been having a blast with Beastmaster. While it can be a bit tedious to level at times, I’d prefer this be something that lasts me a good long while rather than speeding to the current cap of level 50. This’ll probably hold me over until Evercold at least, which is great because I just got all my other jobs to cap after my raiding group disbanded amicably, and I need things to do. Hope you enjoyed the read, and I’ll see you again next patch.
